Color and Numeric Representations

MaterialPracticeQuiz

Use the desk drawing to see how the same stored numbers can mean different colours. Build explicit conversion habits before editing any pixel values.

What you will learn

  • Distinguish channel order from array shape and numeric range.
  • Convert RGB to grayscale and interpret OpenCV HSV conventions.
  • Promote, clip and round image arithmetic deliberately.
  • Inspect signed differences and quantify colour quantization.

Before this lab: Complete Lab 01 and be comfortable with array indexing and simple NumPy arithmetic.

In this lab

  1. RGB and BGR channel order
  2. Dtypes and numeric ranges
  3. Grayscale weighting
  4. HSV conventions
  5. Saturation as a separate edit
  6. Overflow and clipping
  7. Signed difference maps
  8. Quantization and recoverability

Prepare your notebook

Use a Python notebook with OpenCV, Pillow, NumPy and Matplotlib. Run the setup once, then run the guided blocks in order. The copy button selects only the code.

The examples were checked with OpenCV 4.13, Pillow 12.3, NumPy 2.2 and Matplotlib 3.11. The repository’s Python requirements list the versions. These pages and images open offline; running the code requires the Python libraries.

Run this setup once. rgb is a writable uint8 RGB array with shape (128,192,3); scene is the matching Pillow drawing.

Python · shared setup
import io
from pathlib import Path
import tempfile
import numpy as np
import cv2
from PIL import Image, ImageDraw, ImageOps, UnidentifiedImageError
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
cv2.setNumThreads(1)

# Original 192-by-128 desk drawing with text, fine lines and a textured background.
h, w = 128, 192
yy, xx = np.mgrid[:h, :w]
wood = 180 + 18*xx/(w-1) + 6*np.sin(yy*0.7) + 3*np.sin(xx*0.23)
background = np.stack([wood+20, wood, wood-28], axis=-1)
scene = Image.fromarray(np.clip(background,0,255).astype(np.uint8))
draw = ImageDraw.Draw(scene)
draw.rectangle((12,20,80,108), fill=(166,45,52), outline=(72,25,31), width=2)
draw.rectangle((14,22,23,106), fill=(105,32,44))
draw.rectangle((26,32,72,56), fill=(239,228,198))
draw.text((31,39),"NOTES", fill=(35,42,52))
for y in range(92,107,3):

draw.rectangle((88,7,127,43),fill=(241,216,82),outline=(148,115,29))
draw.text((94,13),"TO DO",fill=(45,44,31))

The image comparisons below come from the guided code. Use their captions and shared display scales to compare each change.

Guided task 01

RGB and BGR channel order

A shape such as (128,192,3) tells us that there are three numbers at each location, but it does not name those numbers. Pillow's RGB mode and Matplotlib's three-channel image display use red, green and blue order. OpenCV's colour decoder normally returns blue, green and red order. Passing that decoded array directly to an RGB display swaps the interpretation of red and blue without changing its shape or dtype.

Encode our drawing in memory, decode the bytes with OpenCV and explicitly convert BGR to RGB. Keep the incorrectly displayed panel as a controlled comparison, clearly labelled. This is a decoder convention, not a rule that every array touched by OpenCV becomes BGR: resizing or adding values to an explicitly supplied RGB array preserves its channel positions. Conversion should happen at a named boundary, not repeatedly until an image looks familiar. Write the order into variable names when arrays from different libraries meet. A grayscale or unusually neutral image can hide this mistake, so include a visibly coloured object when checking the route.

Try it

  1. Decode the same PNG with OpenCV.
  2. Display the decoded array with and without a channel conversion.
  3. Compare corrected pixels with the original RGB values.
Python · run in order
buffer = io.BytesIO()
scene.save(buffer,format="PNG")
bgr = cv2.imdecode(np.frombuffer(buffer.getvalue(),dtype=np.uint8),cv2.IMREAD_COLOR)
restored_rgb = cv2.cvtColor(bgr,cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1,3,figsize=(11,3))
for ax,image,title in zip(axes,[rgb,bgr,restored_rgb],["Original RGB","BGR shown as RGB: wrong","Converted RGB"]):
    ax.imshow(image)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

The book changes colour in the incorrectly interpreted panel. The corrected panel should agree pixel for pixel because this PNG route preserves the decoded sample values.

Change and compare

  • Inspect the three numbers at a red book pixel before and after conversion.
  • Try the same route after making the drawing grayscale; explain why visual inspection becomes weaker.

Guided task 02

Dtypes and numeric ranges

Integer RGB display values conventionally occupy 0 through 255, whereas floating RGB display values occupy 0 through 1. Converting uint8 to float32 changes how a number is stored; it does not by itself divide the number by 255. Conversely, dividing a correctly scaled float image again compresses its entire range close to zero. Those two mistakes can be hard to spot when only a dtype is printed.

Create a correctly scaled float image and an intentionally double-scaled version. Display both using their actual floating values, not a per-image contrast stretch that would hide the error. The intended conversion is exactly once at this boundary. Keep track of the source range as well as the destination dtype; a downstream consumer may require a different documented range. A float32 array can hold negative numbers, large values and nonfinite values, so its type alone is never proof that it is valid RGB data. Here the original byte fixture supplies the finite, bounded input, and the checks confirm the conversion rather than inferring a contract from appearance.

Try it

  1. Cast the original bytes to float32.
  2. Divide by 255 once, and separately demonstrate an accidental second division.
  3. Inspect both dtype and minimum/maximum values.
Python · run in order
float_bytes = rgb.astype(np.float32)
rgb01 = float_bytes/255.0
double_scaled = rgb01/255.0
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1,3,figsize=(11,3))
for ax,image,title in zip(axes,[rgb,rgb01,double_scaled],["uint8, 0 to 255","float32, 0 to 1","Divided twice"]):
    ax.imshow(image)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()
print("Correct:",rgb01.dtype,float(rgb01.min()),float(rgb01.max()))
print("Twice:",float(double_scaled.min()),float(double_scaled.max()))

Read the result

The byte image and correctly scaled float image have the same intended appearance. The third panel is dark because floating RGB values are interpreted on a fixed unit scale.

Change and compare

  • Check a pixel containing the byte value 180 before and after scaling.
  • Multiply the valid float image by 255 and round before converting it back to bytes.

Guided task 03

Grayscale weighting

Reducing RGB to one intensity channel is a choice about which information to retain. OpenCV's standard RGB-to-gray conversion uses weights near 0.299 for red, 0.587 for green and 0.114 for blue, with integer rounding for byte input. It therefore differs from giving all three channels equal weight. Coloured objects can have different grayscale values even when their simple channel averages match.

Compare the standard conversion with a rounded arithmetic mean of the three channels. Display both on the same 0–255 grayscale limits; otherwise independent display scaling could exaggerate or conceal their differences. The difference map is calculated after promotion to a signed type. These operations act on the supplied encoded channel values and are not a physically exact linear-light luminance measurement. Neither image can reconstruct the discarded colour channels. Choose a grayscale route because the next operation needs that representation, and retain the original RGB data if colour still matters to the eventual task. A red label and a blue label can lose an important distinction after conversion.

Try it

  1. Convert RGB with COLOR_RGB2GRAY.
  2. Construct an equally weighted mean image.
  3. Compare their absolute difference using safe subtraction.
Python · run in order
gray = cv2.cvtColor(rgb,cv2.COLOR_RGB2GRAY)
mean_gray = np.rint(rgb.astype(np.float32).mean(axis=2)).astype(np.uint8)
gray_difference = np.abs(gray.astype(np.int16)-mean_gray.astype(np.int16))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1,3,figsize=(11,3))
axes[0].imshow(gray,cmap="gray",vmin=0,vmax=255)
axes[0].set_title("Weighted grayscale")
axes[1].imshow(mean_gray,cmap="gray",vmin=0,vmax=255)
axes[1].set_title("Equal channel mean")
im = axes[2].imshow(gray_difference,cmap="magma",vmin=0,vmax=60)
axes[2].set_title("Absolute byte difference")
fig.colorbar(im,ax=axes[2],shrink=0.7)
for ax in axes:
    ax.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

Differences are tied to the scene's colours, rather than its array dimensions. The common grayscale limits make the two intensity images directly comparable.

Change and compare

  • Compare the gray values of pure red, green and blue swatches.
  • Use a neutral RGB pixel with equal channels and check whether the two methods agree.

Guided task 04

HSV conventions

HSV separates a colour's hue, saturation and value into channels with different meanings. For OpenCV's standard uint8 conversion, hue uses integer codes from 0 through 179, while saturation and value use 0 through 255. The hue circle wraps around, so nearby reds can lie on opposite sides of the numeric boundary. A zero-saturation pixel has no meaningful hue even though an implementation must store a number there.

Inspect each channel separately instead of displaying the three-channel HSV array as if it were RGB. The colour map used to show hue is an explanatory display choice, not the original image. The value channel is the maximum of the input RGB channels, which makes it different from the weighted grayscale intensity introduced above. Floating-point HSV follows another range convention: hue is in degrees, while saturation and value use unit values when RGB input was correctly normalized. Record both dtype and convention before applying thresholds or interpreting numbers. Do not carry a byte hue boundary unchanged into floating HSV code.

Try it

  1. Convert the byte RGB drawing to HSV.
  2. Display hue, saturation and value with stated limits.
  3. Check the hue codes of three known primary-colour swatches.
Python · run in order
hsv = cv2.cvtColor(rgb,cv2.COLOR_RGB2HSV)
swatches = np.array([[[255,0,0],[0,255,0],[0,0,255]]],dtype=np.uint8)
swatch_hsv = cv2.cvtColor(swatches,cv2.COLOR_RGB2HSV)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1,4,figsize=(12,3))
axes[0].imshow(rgb)
axes[0].set_title("RGB")
axes[1].imshow(hsv[:,:,0],cmap="hsv",vmin=0,vmax=179)
axes[1].set_title("Hue codes 0 to 179")
axes[2].imshow(hsv[:,:,1],cmap="gray",vmin=0,vmax=255)
axes[2].set_title("Saturation 0 to 255")
axes[3].imshow(hsv[:,:,2],cmap="gray",vmin=0,vmax=255)
axes[3].set_title("Value 0 to 255")
for ax in axes:
    ax.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()
print("Red, green, blue hue codes:",swatch_hsv[0,:,0])

Read the result

The value image is bright wherever any RGB channel is strong. Hue colours are only a visualization, and hue in nearly neutral regions should not be treated as reliable colour evidence.

Change and compare

  • Compare the book's hue and saturation with those of the pale mug.
  • Convert unit-range float RGB to HSV and inspect the changed channel ranges.

Guided task 05

Saturation as a separate edit

A colour edit should name which representation and channels it changes. Reduce only the saturation channel of HSV, leaving hue and value codes unchanged, then convert the result back to RGB for display. This makes a useful controlled experiment: we can see the effect of weakening colour while keeping the HSV value channel fixed.

Perform arithmetic in floating point, clip to the byte range and round before casting. Integer conversion and colour-space conversion introduce quantization, so do not assume an RGB-to-HSV-to-RGB round trip is exact for every colour. A second version sets saturation to zero. Its three RGB channels become equal to the retained value, rather than to weighted grayscale. That distinction explains why removing saturation this way is not interchangeable with COLOR_RGB2GRAY. The edit also removes distinctions that may carry meaning, such as a coloured tab identifying a notebook. A visually calmer result is a stylistic change, not evidence of better information for a later system. Preserve the source and make the chosen factor explicit.

Try it

  1. Create independent HSV copies.
  2. Scale saturation by 0.35 in one copy and set it to zero in another.
  3. Convert both edited arrays back to RGB for comparison.
Python · run in order
source_hsv = cv2.cvtColor(rgb,cv2.COLOR_RGB2HSV)
muted_hsv = source_hsv.copy()
muted_hsv[:,:,1] = np.rint(np.clip(source_hsv[:,:,1].astype(np.float32)*0.35,0,255)).astype(np.uint8)
neutral_hsv = source_hsv.copy()
neutral_hsv[:,:,1] = 0
muted = cv2.cvtColor(muted_hsv,cv2.COLOR_HSV2RGB)
neutral_value = cv2.cvtColor(neutral_hsv,cv2.COLOR_HSV2RGB)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1,3,figsize=(11,3))
for ax,image,title in zip(axes,[rgb,muted,neutral_value],["Original","Saturation times 0.35","Zero saturation, retain V"]):
    ax.imshow(image)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

The middle panel keeps some colour, while the last panel has equal RGB channels. The last image can differ from weighted grayscale because it retains maximum-channel value.

Change and compare

  • Compare zero-saturation HSV conversion with weighted grayscale.
  • Try a factor of 0.7 and record which channel arrays remain unchanged.

Guided task 06

Overflow and clipping

A byte can represent only 256 different unsigned values. NumPy arithmetic performed in uint8 can wrap around that limited range, so adding brightness directly may turn a bright channel into a dark one. That is a numeric storage effect, not a plausible brightening rule. Saturating arithmetic instead stops at the largest allowed value.

Compare an intentionally wrapping addition with an explicit promote-add-clip-cast route. Promotion must happen before the addition; casting the already wrapped result cannot recover the lost value. Clipping itself also loses information: several different bright input values can all become 255. Count the affected channel samples and inspect where the scene flattens. This count describes the chosen operation on the drawing, not its visual quality. Different libraries can have different arithmetic policies, so specify the policy instead of transferring an assumption from one API to another. Keeping intermediate computations in a wider type makes the sequence visible and gives you a place to inspect values before enforcing the output range.

Try it

  1. Add 40 with byte arithmetic as a labelled failure example.
  2. Repeat after promoting to int16 and clipping to 0–255.
  3. Count channel samples whose unclipped result exceeds 255.
Python · run in order
wrapped = np.add(rgb,np.uint8(40),dtype=np.uint8)
wide = rgb.astype(np.int16)+40
safe_bright = np.clip(wide,0,255).astype(np.uint8)
clipped_channels = int(np.count_nonzero(wide>255))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1,3,figsize=(11,3))
for ax,image,title in zip(axes,[rgb,wrapped,safe_bright],["Original","uint8 addition: wraps","Promote, add, clip"]):
    ax.imshow(image)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()
print("Clipped channel samples:",clipped_channels)

Read the result

Some formerly bright areas become dark in the wrapping result. The clipped result follows the stated brightening rule, but its saturated areas have lost differences between bright values.

Change and compare

  • Apply a negative offset in int16 and inspect clipping at zero.
  • Find two distinct input byte values that both become 255 after adding 40.

Guided task 07

Signed difference maps

Subtracting two images asks a directional question. Here a negative difference means that a channel became darker, and a positive difference means it became brighter. An unsigned output cannot express the negative half of that information. Convert both operands before subtraction and retain a signed result until you deliberately choose another summary.

Create a version of the desk with a negative offset on the left and a positive offset on the right. After output clipping, compute modified minus original in int16 and average the three signed channel changes for display. A diverging colour map with symmetric limits places zero at the middle, making the direction interpretable. The mean is a display summary, not a claim that all channels changed equally after clipping. An absolute difference would answer how large the change was while discarding its direction; choose it only when that is the question. A difference map is not an object mask, an edge detector or a probability map, even when its strongest areas outline visible objects.

Try it

  1. Darken the left half by 35 and brighten the right half by 20.
  2. Subtract original values after promoting both arrays.
  3. Display the average signed channel change on symmetric limits.
Python · run in order
adjustment = np.full((h,w,1),20,dtype=np.int16)
adjustment[:,:w//2] = -35
modified = np.clip(rgb.astype(np.int16)+adjustment,0,255).astype(np.uint8)
signed_change = modified.astype(np.int16)-rgb.astype(np.int16)
mean_change = signed_change.mean(axis=2)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1,3,figsize=(11,3))
axes[0].imshow(rgb)
axes[0].set_title("Original")
axes[1].imshow(modified)
axes[1].set_title("Left -35; right +20")
im = axes[2].imshow(mean_change,cmap="coolwarm",vmin=-35,vmax=35)
axes[2].set_title("Mean signed channel change")
fig.colorbar(im,ax=axes[2],shrink=0.7)
for ax in axes:
    ax.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

The sign separates darkening from brightening. Clipping near black or white can make the actual change smaller than the requested offset.

Change and compare

  • Swap the subtraction order and explain the new signs.
  • Compare the signed map with an absolute map without calling either one a probability.

Guided task 08

Quantization and recoverability

Quantization maps many possible values to a smaller set of representable levels. A byte channel already has 256 levels; reducing it to eight deliberately makes the effect easier to inspect. Convert to unit floats, round to the nearest one of eight levels and map those levels back into the byte range for display. The number of levels and the number of intervals differ: eight endpoints span seven equal intervals.

The smooth desk background and fine shaded details reveal where nearby input values merge. Compute absolute error from the original bytes after safe promotion, then show the largest channel error at each pixel. A low-looking error map does not make quantization reversible. Once different values have collapsed to the same code, converting that code to float32 merely represents the reduced information in another type. The display can also hide subtle differences at its chosen size, which is why both numeric and visual inspection matter. This exercise concerns numeric representation, not an encoder's file-size guarantee or a model's accuracy. Keep the original array when experimenting with reduced precision.

Try it

  1. Quantize each unit-range channel to eight equally spaced levels.
  2. Round the reconstructed values back into byte storage.
  3. Compare the image with a maximum-channel absolute error map.
Python · run in order
unit_rgb = rgb.astype(np.float32)/255.0
level_codes = np.rint(unit_rgb*7)
quantized = np.rint(level_codes/7*255).astype(np.uint8)
quant_error = np.max(np.abs(quantized.astype(np.int16)-rgb.astype(np.int16)),axis=2)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1,3,figsize=(11,3))
axes[0].imshow(rgb)
axes[0].set_title("Original byte RGB")
axes[1].imshow(quantized)
axes[1].set_title("Eight levels per channel")
im = axes[2].imshow(quant_error,cmap="magma",vmin=0,vmax=19)
axes[2].set_title("Largest channel error")
fig.colorbar(im,ax=axes[2],shrink=0.7)
for ax in axes:
    ax.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

The texture can show visible bands, while the error map measures the actual per-pixel change. A float conversion of the quantized result cannot recreate the discarded original distinctions.

Change and compare

  • Use 16 levels and compare the number of possible output codes.
  • Inspect a gradient crop at larger display size without changing its stored resolution.
